headings.title: Introduction and Classification of Antipsychotic Drugs
headings.content: Antipsychotic drugs are foundational pharmacotherapeutic agents used primarily in the management of severe psychiatric disorders characterized by psychosis, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and acute psychotic episodes. In Nigerian psychiatric nursing practice, understanding these medications is crucial for promoting mental health recovery and ensuring safe patient care. Historically referred to as major tranquilizers or neuroleptics, antipsychotics are broadly categorized into two major classes based on their chemical structure, receptor affinity profile, and side effect tendencies: first-generation (typical) antipsychotics and second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics. First-generation antipsychotics were developed earlier and are well known for their high potency in blocking dopamine pathways, which effectively controls positive symptoms like hallucinations and delusions. However, they carry a high risk of movement disorders. In contrast, second-generation antipsychotics were introduced later and serve as the newer standard of care due to a more favorable neurological profile, though they introduce distinct metabolic challenges. Psychiatric nurses must understand these classifications to anticipate therapeutic responses, educate patients and their families, and collaborate effectively with the multidisciplinary mental health team in clinical settings across Nigeria.

headings.title: Mechanism of Action in the Central Nervous System
headings.content: The therapeutic efficacy and adverse effect profile of antipsychotic drugs are directly tied to their pharmacological mechanisms within the central nervous system. The core pathology of psychosis is heavily linked to dysregulation of neurotransmitters, particularly dopamine. First-generation antipsychotics act primarily as strong antagonists at the dopamine D2 receptors located in various pathways of the brain, notably the mesolimbic pathway. By blocking these receptors, they reduce the hyperactive dopaminergic transmission responsible for positive symptoms of schizophrenia, such as hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking. However, because D2 antagonism is widespread, it also affects the nigrostriatal, tuberoinfundibular, and mesocortical pathways, leading to unwanted neurological and endocrine side effects. Second-generation antipsychotics, on the other hand, exhibit a different mechanism by blocking both dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors simultaneously. This combined serotonin-dopamine antagonism helps mitigate the risk of movement disorders seen with older drugs while addressing both positive and potentially negative symptoms of psychosis. Understanding these intricate central nervous system pathways enables nursing students to connect a patient's physical symptoms directly to the pharmacological action of their prescribed medication.

headings.title: First-Generation (Typical) Antipsychotics
headings.content: First-generation antipsychotics (FGAs), also known as typical antipsychotics, represent the older class of neuroleptic medications. Classic examples commonly prescribed or encountered in psychiatric practice include haloperidol, chlorpromazine, and fluphenazine. These drugs are highly effective in subduing the acute positive symptoms of schizophrenia, such as agitation, combativeness, delusions, and auditory hallucinations. Because of their potency and availability in long-acting depot formulations, they are frequently utilized in emergency psychiatric care and in resource-constrained settings across Nigeria for rapid tranquilization and maintenance therapy. Despite their clinical utility, FGAs are notorious for causing a high incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) due to non-selective blockade of dopamine receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway. They can also cause anticholinergic side effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, as well as neuroendocrine disturbances like hyperprolactinemia. Psychiatric nurses administering FGAs must remain highly vigilant, conducting thorough baseline and ongoing neurological assessments to identify early signs of movement disorders before they become debilitating or permanent.

headings.title: Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics
headings.content: Second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs), commonly referred to as atypical antipsychotics, include medications such as clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, and ziprasidone. Developed after typical antipsychotics, SGAs are considered first-line treatment for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders in many modern psychiatric settings because they effectively treat both positive and negative symptoms (such as apathy, social withdrawal, and blunted affect) while carrying a significantly lower risk of extrapyramidal symptoms. However, SGAs are associated with a distinct profile of adverse effects, primarily metabolic syndrome. This includes significant weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus. Clozapine, a unique atypical agent, is exceptionally effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia but requires rigorous monitoring of white blood cell counts due to the severe risk of agranulocytosis. Psychiatric nurses play a vital role in educating patients on lifestyle modifications, monitoring baseline and follow-up metabolic parameters like fasting blood glucose and lipid profiles, and ensuring adherence to mandatory blood monitoring protocols when specific SGAs are prescribed.

headings.title: Indications and Clinical Uses in Psychiatric Nursing
headings.content: Antipsychotic medications have diverse indications and clinical uses across various psychiatric specialties. While their primary FDA-approved and clinical indication is the management of schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, they are also widely prescribed for acute manic episodes in bipolar disorder, treatment-resistant depression with psychotic features, and severe agitation associated with dementia or delirium. In some clinical scenarios, low doses of specific antipsychotics are used off-label for severe anxiety, insomnia, or behavioral disturbances in neurodevelopmental disorders. Psychiatric nurses must understand these indications to evaluate whether a patient's prescribed regimen aligns with their specific psychiatric diagnosis. Furthermore, nurses assess therapeutic effectiveness by observing changes in the patient's thought processes, mood stability, level of reality contact, and social functioning. Patient education regarding the rationale for long-term therapy is essential, as many individuals with chronic mental illnesses require maintenance antipsychotic treatment to prevent relapse and psychiatric hospitalization. Nurses provide this ongoing support within hospital wards, community mental health clinics, and outpatient departments throughout Nigeria.

headings.title: Adverse Effects and Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS)
headings.content: Adverse effects of antipsychotics can significantly impact patient compliance and quality of life. Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) are among the most prominent movement-related complications, particularly with first-generation agents. EPS manifest in several distinct forms: acute dystonia (painful muscle spasms of the neck, jaw, and tongue occurring hours to days after initiation), akathisia (a distressing inner sense of motor restlessness and inability to sit still), pseudoparkinsonism (resting tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait, and mask-like facies), and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary, repetitive choreoathetoid movements of the tongue, face, and extremities, which can become permanent if the offending drug is not withdrawn). In addition to EPS, nurses must monitor for autonomic and endocrine adverse effects such as anticholinergic symptoms (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation), orthostatic hypotension, sedation, sexual dysfunction, and hyperprolactinemia leading to galactorrhea or gynecomastia. Early identification of these symptoms using standardized rating scales and prompt reporting to the attending physician allows for timely interventions, such as dose adjustment or the administration of anticholinergic antiparkinsonian agents like benztropine.

headings.title: Management of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
headings.content: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) is a rare, highly lethal, and medical emergency neurological complication associated with the use of antipsychotic medications, more commonly seen with high-potency first-generation agents. NMS is characterized by a tetrad of clinical features: severe hyperthermia (extreme fever), 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, altered mental status (ranging from confusion to coma), and autonomic instability (manifested by labile blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and tachypnea). Laboratory findings often reveal elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) due to rhabdomyolysis, leukocytosis, and myoglobinuria. When NMS is suspected, psychiatric nurses must act immediately: discontinue the antipsychotic drug without delay, notify the medical team, and initiate aggressive supportive measures. Supportive care includes rapid cooling measures, maintaining adequate hydration and electrolyte balance, and providing respiratory support if necessary. Specific pharmacological treatments, such as dantrolene (a muscle relaxant) or bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist), may be ordered to reverse the neurological blockade. Prompt recognition and intensive nursing intervention are critical to reducing mortality and preventing permanent organ damage.

headings.title: Nursing Responsibilities and Patient Monitoring
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing responsibilities and patient monitoring are essential for safe pharmacotherapy with antipsychotics. Nurses must perform thorough baseline assessments—including vital signs, mental status exams, weight, waist circumference, fasting blood glucose, lipid profile, and neurological status—before medication administration begins. Ongoing monitoring involves regular checks for therapeutic efficacy, medication adherence, and the emergence of both common and severe adverse effects. Because orthostatic hypotension is a frequent risk, nurses should teach patients to change positions slowly and monitor blood pressure regularly. For patients taking clozapine, nurses must strictly adhere to protocols for monitoring absolute neutrophil counts (ANC) to guard against agranulocytosis. Furthermore, nurses provide individualized patient and family education regarding the importance of adherence, managing minor side effects like dry mouth or constipation through diet and hydration, and knowing when to report dangerous symptoms such as high fever, muscle stiffness, or suicidal ideation. Documenting all assessments and interventions accurately ensures continuity of care across mental health facilities in Nigeria.
